Log ratio of standard deviations

Source: R/two_period_covs.R
log_ratio_sd.Rd

Computes the log of the ratio of the standard deviation of a covariate for the treated group to its standard deviation for the untreated group, optionally after applying estimation weights. This unit-free balance statistic compares the spread of the two distributions (Imbens and Rubin, 2015); it is zero when the spreads are equal.

Usage

log_ratio_sd(
  x,
  D,
  est_weights = rep(1, length(x)),
  sampling_weights = rep(1, length(x))
)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector.

D

A binary vector, 1 for treated and 0 for untreated units.

est_weights

A numeric vector of weights from an estimation procedure (e.g., implicit regression or AIPW weights). Default rep(1, length(x)) (unweighted).

sampling_weights

A numeric vector of sampling weights. Default rep(1, length(x)).

Value

A number, \(\log(sd_1) - \log(sd_0)\), or NA (see Details).

Details

Within each group, each unit is weighted by the product of its estimation weight and its sampling weight, and the standard deviation is the weighted standard deviation with the usual small-sample correction for weights, \(\sum_i w_i (x_i - \bar{x}_w)^2 / (\sum_i w_i - \sum_i w_i^2 / \sum_i w_i)\). With equal weights this is the ordinary sample standard deviation, so the unweighted statistic is the one in Imbens and Rubin (2015). The result does not depend on the scale of the weights.

The statistic is NA when either standard deviation is not defined: for example, when a group has a single unit, when a covariate is constant within a group, or when negative estimation weights (which implicit regression and AIPW weights can have) make the weighted variance negative.

References

Imbens, Guido W. and Donald B. Rubin. Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences. Cambridge University Press (2015).

Examples

set.seed(1)
D <- rep(c(1, 0), times = c(20, 80))
x <- rnorm(100, sd = 1 + D)
log_ratio_sd(x, D) # about log(2)
#> [1] -0.02304912
